**Conversation Overview**

Steve Schneider is a Professor at SUNY Polytechnic Institute, Co-Director of the Artificial Intelligence Exploration (AIX) Center, and SUNY AI for the Public Good Fellow 2025–2026. He is planning a multi-country Africa trip in May–June with two colleagues, Nick (gaming and AI focus) and Bill, visiting Nigeria (Abuja, May 15–19, with NUC and NOUN meetings via contact Adebayo Adegboyega) and Cameroon (Buea May 25–26 via contact Nkweteyim Denis at University of Buea; Yaoundé May 28–29 via contact Edwin Mbinkar at University of Yaoundé I). He flies home June 2, arriving Newark June 3, needing to be upstate by June 3–4 ahead of the NYHIMA conference June 7–10 at Vernon Downs where he speaks June 8. The trip supports a six-stream partnership across four institutions: NOUN and FUT Minna (Nigeria), University of Buea and University of Yaoundé I (Cameroon), covering AI literacy OER, LLM benchmarking, AI academic tutoring, precision agriculture with drones, health access applications, and advanced manufacturing with medical 3D printing.

The conversation covered Cameroon tourist and professional opportunities extensively. Steve wants to meet people where they work, live, and play — explicitly contrasting this with a prior Ghana trip where he felt he did not take full advantage. Key sites identified: BLIS Global Center (Biyem-Assi Lac, Yaoundé; kids programming robots and 3D printing; contact cameroon@blisglobal.tech, +237 677 980 934), Cameroon Flying Labs (drone/AI/robotics projects with University of Yaoundé I's Computer Science department since 2020; operates weekdays, compatible with his schedule), Silicon Mountain tech ecosystem in Buea, GDG Yaoundé (Google Developer Group, runs AI workshops, WhatsApp community), and Wikimedians of Cameroon (formally recognized Wikimedia user group active in Yaoundé, Douala, Buea, and Maroua). Steve developed a strong interest in the intersection of Wikipedia and AI — specifically that communities undocumented on Wikipedia are absent from LLM training data, making Wikipedia editing an AI literacy intervention. This framing connects to his Living with AI project, AAC&U conference work, and AIX Center programming. RAI-MULTILAB at University of Yaoundé II (raimultilab@univ-yaounde2.org) was identified as a near-perfect institutional partner, with five research axes mapping directly to his six project streams, and connections to AI4PEP (Canada-Africa health AI initiative) and Dr. Jude Kong. Julius Angwah (University of Yaoundé I, HTTC English Department) was identified as a potential contact based on published AI literacy research from Steve's host institution. The CFA franc exchange rate is approximately 550–560 XAF per USD. Late May is rainy season in both Buea and Yaoundé; mornings are best for outdoor activities.

A three-day post-work weekend itinerary was sketched for May 30 (Saturday), May 31 (Sunday), and June 1 (Monday) in Yaoundé, oriented around tech entrepreneur meetups, GDG community, a potential Wikipedia edit-a-thon on Cameroon's tech scene, BLIS Global visit, Mefou Primate Sanctuary, Maison Blanche restaurant, and Le Safoutier for high-end dining. Google's Africa programs were discussed including 100,000 free career certificates across Africa in 2026 and the AfCFTA digital inclusion program; Steve noted SUNY Poly also runs Google Career Certificates. The SUNY Empire model of accepting ACE-credited Coursera certificates toward degree credits was identified as a potential template for a Cameroon-SUNY articulation pathway. content.text:
Late May is **rainy season** in both cities — here's what to expect:

**Yaoundé** (elevation ~2,500 ft)
- Temps range 66–87°F year-round, warm and humid
- Late May: daily afternoon thunderstorms typical, mornings usually clear
- Expect t-storms in the p.m. — plan outdoor stuff for mornings

**Buea** (base of Mount Cameroon, ~3,000 ft)
- Temps 63–80°F, wet season is comfortable but overcast
- Cooler than Yaoundé, but significantly wetter — this is one of the rainiest places in Africa
- Mount Cameroon hikes in late May: possible but muddy and cloudy

**Bottom line for planning:**
- Pack light rain gear — not heavy, just a packable jacket and quick-dry clothes
- Morning windows are your best bet for outdoor activities
- Kribi beach is rain-season too, but the Lobe waterfalls are actually more dramatic with high water
- Buea/Mount Cameroon in late May is ambitious — rain and cloud cover are heavy

content.text:
This is actually rich territory for you. Here's the picture:

**The hub geography**

Three main nodes: **ActivSpaces** in Douala, **Mountain Hub** in Yaoundé, and **Silicon Mountain** in Buea — where you already have meetings at University of Buea. Silicon Mountain sits on the slopes of Mount Cameroon and draws from two universities and a young, tech-savvy demographic.

**AI at the national level**

Cameroon launched its National AI Strategy (SNIA) in Yaoundé in July, targeting 60,000 AI professionals by 2040, 12,000 direct jobs, and a local LLM called **GPT Cameroon** built on national languages.

**Street level**

In Yaoundé, kids as young as four are pitching AI projects at the **Kitadis boot camp** — one team built a meal-planning tool inspired by a pregnant mother's struggle. At **BLIS Global Center** in Biyem-Assi, kids arrive in lab coats at 8am to program robots and use 3D printers.

**Connectivity reality check**

About 42% of Cameroonians are online — slightly above the African average — but quality access is concentrated in Douala and Yaoundé, with rural areas still facing slow and expensive connectivity.

**For you specifically**

- **Silicon Mountain / Buea** is the most concentrated tech scene and you're already going there for U Buea — worth asking Nkweteyim Denis about connecting with that community
- **Mountain Hub in Yaoundé** would be a natural drop-in after your Edwin Mbinkar meetings
- The SNIA / GPT Cameroon angle connects directly to your AI literacy and multilingual work — good conversation material with every institution you're visiting

This one is genuinely exciting for you.

**What they do**

Cameroon Flying Labs uses drones, robotics, and AI to address community needs in health, agriculture, conservation, and infrastructure. They train university students and run youth robotics programs. Real projects include powerline inspection, land surveys, and crop management.

**The University of Yaoundé I connection**

They've been working with the Department of Computer Science at University of Yaoundé I since 2020 — teaching drone computing, mobile app development to control drones, AI, machine learning, and computer vision using live drone feeds. That's Edwin Mbinkar's institution. Direct overlap.

**Real-world AI in the field**

Drone-collected data feeds into dashboards to monitor climate impacts. Their model emphasizes deep stakeholder engagement — government, civil society, academia — with community engagement representing roughly half of all project work.

As recently as January 2026, they mentored five young innovators who won a gold medal in a competition.

**Disaster + health applications**

They've mapped flood-prone areas in Douala using aerial imagery, handing data directly to local authorities for infrastructure decisions. That's AI in public health and disaster management — live, not theoretical.

**For you**

This is the countryside/hospitals/factories thread made airborne. Drones mapping landslides, inspecting powerlines, supporting crop management in rural areas — all AI-driven, all community-embedded. And they already work with your host institution. Ask Edwin to connect you with the Flying Labs coordinator directly.

content.text: Interesting angle. Wikipedia and ai don’t meet

Exactly. That's the tension worth naming.

Wikipedia is one of the most important knowledge sources in the world — and it runs on human editors, notability standards, citation requirements, consensus. Deliberately non-AI.

But AI runs on Wikipedia. Every major LLM trained on it. GPT Cameroon — the local language model in Cameroon's national AI strategy — will train on whatever exists in Cameroonian languages and about Cameroon on Wikipedia. If the tech scene, the local languages, the rural health systems aren't documented there, they don't exist in the training data.

**The angle:**
What gets documented on Wikipedia shapes what AI knows. Communities that don't write themselves into Wikipedia get written out of AI's world model. That's an AI literacy argument, not just a Wikipedia argument.

For Cameroon specifically — 250 native languages, a national AI strategy building a local LLM, a tech ecosystem that's barely documented in English let alone French or Cameroonian languages — the stakes are concrete.

**For you this is:**
- A Living with AI episode
- An AAC&U conference frame — Wikipedia as AI pre-training infrastructure
- A Saturday workshop hook that's intellectually sharp, not just skill-building
- A bridge between the Wikimedians of Cameroon and the GDG community who don't currently overlap much

Here are the key links and the honest picture:

**The SUNY Empire model**

- SUNY Empire partnered with NYS Department of Labor and Coursera to create a degree pathway — Google, IBM, Salesforce certificates completed on Coursera count toward any of 125 bachelor's and associate degree programs. → sunyempire.edu/mkt/dol-coursera

- Specifically: courses with ACE Credit Recommendation on Coursera can count for 1–18 credits toward a SUNY Empire degree. → blog.coursera.org (Coursera's announcement)

**The international wall**

SUNY Empire does accept transcripts from some international institutions — but only Israeli institutions and Canadian institutions are explicitly listed as pre-approved without foreign credential evaluation. Cameroon is not on the list. So the pathway exists in principle but has a bureaucratic gap for African learners.

**The ACE Credit angle is the real door**

The certificates themselves — Google AI Essentials, IBM Data Analytics etc. — carry ACE Credit Recommendations regardless of where you completed them. That's not SUNY-specific. Any institution that accepts ACE credits could theoretically recognize them. The question is whether University of Buea or University of Yaoundé I could adopt a similar recognition model locally — that's the conversation to have with Edwin and Nkweteyim, and potentially with SUNY Empire's international office before you go.

That's a concrete partnership agenda item worth one email before May.

**The team is Steve, Nick, Bill** — plus Adebayo and Talhah are already at Poly, flying home separately presumably. So the in-country team is the three of you.

**COIL is now live** — Hope Windle is engaged, Solomon Fache is in Abuja, and Hope's proposed structure — two 3-week workshop series, first before you leave, second while you're in-country — means your professors in Nigeria and Cameroon could be co-designing curriculum while you're physically sitting with them. That's powerful.

**Solomon Fache in Abuja** — that's your early arrival answer. If you get to Abuja May 15–17, Solomon is there. He's not a COIL trainer but he's a connector — he can bring the right Nigerian university people into a room. That's your Saturday or Sunday in Abuja right there. Not tourism. People.

**The Abuja weekend question you were asking** — now has a cleaner answer: meet Solomon, meet whoever he convenes, see what Abuja actually looks like for the people you're partnering with. Nick films it. Bill observes. You facilitate.

Want to sketch the Abuja arrival days with that frame?

and, in the email, invite him to attend our monthly meeting on 930 monday morning?

invite hope to attend that meeting as well, to pitch coil. now, thats an idea!

Hope, it would be wonderful if you could join us to introduce COIL directly to the group and sketch what a workshop series might look like for our four partner institutions. Hearing it from you, in conversation with the partners themselves, would be far more useful than any summary I could give.

Solomon, I've just written to you separately — but I wanted you on this thread as a full participant in the conversation, not just a contact. Your perspective on the Nigerian university landscape will be valuable to the whole group.

Please let me know if Monday mornings work for your schedules and we'll get a date on the calendar.

Steve

—
Steven M. Schneider
Professor, SUNY Polytechnic Institute
Co-Director, Artificial Intelligence Exploration (AIX) Center
SUNY AI for the Public Good Fellow, 2025–2026"
    }
  ]
}

Both drafts ready. A few notes:

Email 2 does the quiet work — "full participant in the conversation, not just a contact" signals to both Hope and Solomon how you're framing this. Hope will read that and understand.

Share with Bill, send Solomon first, then send the joint one after he's had a day to see his individual email. Sequencing matters.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the opportunities for under-resourced languages of Cameroon: Experiences from the BASAL programme and the NACALCO Center for Applied Linguistics in Cameroon
September 2024
Conference: International Conference: ‘Dynamiques multilingues et multiculturelles dans le monde : Etudes linguistiques, sociolinguistiques, pédagogiques et didactiques.’ University of Yaoundé 1, ACETELACH, & ANACLAC.At: Yaoundé (Cameroon)
Authors:

SOAS University of London
Patrice Yemmene
University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee
Jacquis Welaze
Request full-text

To read the full-text of this research, you can request a copy directly from the authors.
Abstract
A major preoccupation in the development and preservation of minority languages, especially int eh Global South, is to ascertain how the various efforts by linguists and researchers have impacted or are impacting the future of those languages, in a world that is fast globalising with many of the under-resourced languages becoming the collateral losses of this Globalisation centered on, and led by, dominant forces and institutions from the Global North. In the early 2000s, Maurice Tadadjeu and his team of linguists and socilinguists developed a very ambitious, pan-African applied linguistics project aimed at creating sustainable foundations for a boosting of local-language literacy in Africa: The Basic Standardization of All African Languages (BASAL). The project goal was to achieve basic standardization through a set of applied linguistic activities for African languages without an orthography and a writing system. Several young African linguists were deployed in the field where they carried out, within three years, successful linguistic standardization activities that contributed significantly, among many other things, to the description and development of the chosen languages. Linguistic activities included (but were not limited to): sociolinguistic analysis, phonetic analysis, phonological description, morphological analysis, grammatical description (to produce and propose a language alphabet and a writing system). A key question that this paper aims to address is the following: Did the Basic Standardization of All Unwritten African Languages (BASAL) program led by the Center of Applied Linguistics of the Cameroon-based National Association of Cameroonian Languages Committees (NACALCO) contribute to the development of artificial intelligence (AI) information systems using Cameroonian Languages? As we look back at the BASAL’s deliverables and consider the basic linguistic requirements for the development of information systems powered by Artificial Intelligence algorithms in low-resourced languages, specifically those related to natural language and speech processing, this paper aims to show how the BASAL programme made significant contributions toward building artificial intelligence (AI) in Cameroonian languages.

Two useful documents. Quick read:

**The ELT/AI paper (Angwah, University of Yaoundé I, 2025)**

This is from your host institution — Julius Angwah is in the Department of English at HTTC, University of Yaoundé I. Edwin Mbinkar's house. Key findings: 51% AI awareness among teachers and students, infrastructure and electricity the top barriers, but 94% professional response rate — meaning educators who engage professionally are more reliably committed than those who engage emotionally. That's a useful frame for your AI literacy work.

**The BASAL/languages paper**

Directly connects to the Wikipedia/AI angle you were developing — 250+ Cameroonian languages, efforts to standardize and document them, and the question of whether that linguistic work feeds into AI training data. GPT Cameroon's viability depends partly on this.

**What this means practically**

Julius Angwah is a potential contact at University of Yaoundé I — ask Edwin to introduce you. He's already thinking about AI in Cameroonian education and publishing on it. That's a conversation, possibly a collaboration.

The BASAL paper authors include someone at SOAS London and someone at University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee — international connections already exist around Cameroonian language documentation and AI. Worth knowing as you think about the Wikipedia/AI literacy angle.

Want me to save these as reference docs for the trip planning file?

AI4PEP Leader Appointed to Scientific Council of Responsible AI Laboratory at University of Yaoundé II: A Landmark for Africa–Canada Collaboration
4 June 2025AI4PEP Projects
The Artificial Intelligence for Pandemic Preparedness and Response (AI4PEP) initiative proudly celebrates a significant milestone in its mission to promote inclusive, ethical, and interdisciplinary approaches to AI. We are delighted to announce that one of AI4PEP’s core leaders, our Executive Director, Dr Jude Kong, has been appointed to the Scientific Council of the newly launched Responsible Artificial Intelligence multidisciplinary Laboratory at the University of Yaoundé II in Cameroon (RAI-MULTILAB UYII).
Pioneering Ethical AI Across Borders
The University of Yaoundé II’s Responsible AI Lab was created as a multidisciplinary hub to explore the ethical, legal, and social dimensions of artificial intelligence in Africa. Its vision aligns deeply with AI4PEP’s values: ensuring that AI is not only a tool for innovation but a force for equity, inclusion, and resilience, especially in the face of global challenges such as pandemics and public health emergencies.
As a member of the lab’s Scientific Council, AI4PEP’s Executive Director will contribute expertise in participatory policy design, ethical AI governance, and transnational knowledge sharing. This role also reinforces AI4PEP’s broader mandate: building bridges across continents to co-design AI systems that serve people first.  Dr Kong expresses this even further as he says; “It is a signal that African and Canadian experts can lead together, not just in times of crisis, but in shaping the future of responsible AI.”
A Collective Vision for Responsible Innovation
At its core, this appointment reflects what AI4PEP stands for: partnerships rooted in mutual respect, co-leadership, and a vision of technology that uplifts rather than divides.
We look forward to working alongside the University of Yaoundé II and the broader RAI-MULTILAB UYII team to drive bold, ethical, and community-based AI solutions. Together, we can build a future where technology reflects the wisdom, resilience, and creativity of the communities it aims to serve.

Good. RAI-MULTILAB is real, active, and well-connected. Key things from their site:

**What they do** — applied responsible AI research, training and mentorship including MOOCs, AI solution development, and strategic advisory for institutions. That's four of your six project streams right there.

**Partners already** — CEIMIA (Montreal AI expertise center) and OpenAIR (African open innovation research network). Canada-Africa bridge is already built.

**Recent activity** — October 2025 cooperation with Polytechnique Dijon, June 2025 working session with OpenAIR network. Active and international.

**Contact** — raimultilab@univ-yaounde2.org, WhatsApp +237 680-79-55-42, address BP 1365 Yaoundé.

**Critical detail** — they're at University of Yaoundé II. Your host Edwin Mbinkar is at University of Yaoundé I. Two separate institutions, probably 20 minutes apart. Worth a deliberate visit, not just a drop-in.

**The ask is simple** — email them before you go, mention your May 28-29 Yaoundé visit, reference the AI4PEP/Dr. Kong connection, and ask for a meeting. Given their Canada partnerships and your SUNY affiliation the conversation will open easily.

Want a draft outreach email?

<p class="has-medium-font-size">Le RAI-MultiLab-UYII agit comme <strong>un carrefour interdisciplinaire</strong> rassemblant chercheurs, étudiants, décideurs publics et partenaires internationaux. Il repose sur la <strong>recherche-action</strong> et vise à résoudre des problèmes concrets tout en générant des connaissances exploitables. Les principes fondamentaux suivants sont au coeur de notre pratique : <strong>collaboration, cycles itératifs, pertinence contextuelle, production des savoirs, flexibilité, et genre, équité et inclusion (GEI)</strong>.</p>

content.text:
Good — their research page confirms their four pillars match your work almost exactly: applied research, training & mentorship, AI solution development, and advisory. Their core principles include collaboration, iterative cycles, contextual relevance, and gender equity & inclusion (GEI) — that last one is notable given your AIX framing.

Their research approach is explicitly action-research rooted in African realities. That's your language too.

One practical note from the page: they list research axes at raimultilab.org/recherche/axes-de-recherche — worth checking before you email them so you can reference specific overlaps.

**Quick summary of what you now have on RAI-MULTILAB:**
- Email: raimultilab@univ-yaounde2.org
- WhatsApp: +237 680-79-55-42
- Located at University of Yaoundé II (separate from Edwin's U Yaoundé I)
- Partners: CEIMIA Montreal, OpenAIR network
- Connected to AI4PEP / Dr. Jude Kong
- Active research + training + MOOC development
- Bilingual French/English institution

Want me to draft the outreach email now?

Excellent. Their five research axes are directly mappable to your work:

**Axe 1** — Co-creation of responsible AI solutions and the future of work in Africa → your AI literacy + OER stream

**Axe 2** — Public policy, law, and scientific diplomacy in AI → your NUC conversations and national AI strategy work

**Axe 3** — Data discoverability, governance, cybersecurity, and digital sovereignty → your LLM benchmarking stream

**Axe 4** — Afrocentric dynamics of AI appropriation and innovation → the Wikipedia/language documentation angle, GPT Cameroon

**Axe 5** — Capacity building, leadership, and skills transfer in AI → your Google certs, AIX Center, COIL work directly

This is a near-perfect alignment. You can reference specific axes in your outreach email rather than speaking generally. That will land very differently than a generic introduction.

Ready to draft the outreach email now — it can be tight and specific.
